/data/api_link	https://api.artic.edu/api/v1/artworks/37423
/data/title	Covered Food Container
/data/date_display	Western Zhou dynasty ( 1046–771 BC ), mid–10th century BC
/data/description	Birds with long, trailing plumage encircle the lid and basin of this vessel. Their flowing lines reflect the skillful hand of the potter who carved the design in clay for casting in bronze. At some time in the past, this extensively damaged vessel was repaired and cleaned, thereby exposing its present, uncorroded surface. Cast in the basin and lid are identical inscriptions: "In the eleventh month, first quarter, [on the day] jiashen, the King was in Hua. The King gave Ming deer. [Ming] therefore made [this] precious vessel. May Ming always [use this] gui to entertain many friends." The unusual inscription describes a secular event, indicating a new use for ritual bronzes. Such commemorative inscriptions, which gradually replaced shorter ancestor dedications, are important documents of Western Zhou history.
/data/medium_display	Bronze
/data/inscriptions	Identical inscriptions cast inside basin and lid: In the eleventh month, first auspiciousness jiashen day, the King was in Hua and the King gave Ming deer. (Ming) therefore made this precious vessel. May Ming always use this gui to offer food to many visitors.
/data/provenance_text	Ton Ying and Company, New York; sold to Kate Sturges Buckingham (1858–1937), Chicago, [Kate served as executor of her sister Lucy Maud Buckingham's estate and continued expanding Lucy's collection following her death in 1920], Nov. 15, 1927; given to the Art Institute of Chicago, Nov. 15, 1927.
/data/department_title	Arts of Asia
